description: We love NASA and space exploration
summary: Fire killed the Apollo 1 crew, and NASA expects Moon-base air at 30% oxygen or more. Station crews cut ventilation to slow a fire; on the Moon, gravity moves warm air again, and that response is untested. Ignos ranks NASA's 24 fire and smoke investigations for your habitat (our judgment, labelled), shows what none of them tested, and adds flame speeds we re-measured from raw BASS-II photos. Its AI answers from cited sources, and code flags any unmatched number.
details:
Ignos (https://ignos.earth) is an SI-powered dashboard for fire safety in human space habitats.

The question: on the space station, crews cut ventilation to slow a fire ("Terminate ventilation in the affected module to slow the spread of fire," NASA OCHMO-TB-008 Rev A, p. 3). On the Moon, gravity moves warm air again, and that response is untested. NASA expects Moon-base air at 30% oxygen or more.

What it does: pick a habitat (ISS, spacecraft cabin, Moon base, Mars base, pressurized rover) and Ignos ranks the 24 NASA PSI investigations related to spacecraft fire and smoke for it, then shows what none of them tested: 0 of the 24 ran at Moon or Mars gravity. The ranking is our judgment, made with AI help and labelled as such. Behind it are three parts:

1. Research. NASA's BASS-II experiment (PSI-25) burned PMMA rods on the station while the crew changed the airflow. The archive has the raw photos but no spread-rate column. Our tracker finds the flame's leading edge in each photo and fits a rate per airflow step, with the scale taken from the rod's own width. At low airflow (below 1 cm/s) our rates are within a median 6.8% of the published rates (Link et al. 2018, Table S1) on 8 steps from 4 tests. Most higher-airflow steps miss, and we show those failures.

2. Moon Gap. NASA's lunar-gravity flammability limits (ICES-2025-392) set against an Earth still-air estimate, per material, with 95% ranges. NASA's lunar tests left Moon airflow unmeasured, and we give no number for it.

3. Ask. A Gemini model answers from our data and the source papers; code checks every number in each answer against a cited source and visibly flags any it cannot match.

Also: live NASA PSI metadata for each investigation, a guided /story tour with the live ISS position, and open code that re-measures the published rates from NASA's raw archive and reproduces our results file byte for byte.

Built with Python (numpy, scipy, rawpy, pytest), TypeScript, React, Vite, Plotly, three.js and Vercel functions. Full method, failures and limits: https://ignos.earth/method
dataRefs: NASA PSI-25 BASS-II raw photos, test videos and experimental table (CC0)
NASA PSI investigations related to spacecraft fire and smoke (24 entries)
ICES-2025-392: lunar-gravity and 1-g flammability limits (Urban, Olson, Dietrich et al.)
FM2: Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity (Ferkul et al., LPSC 2026)
NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Fire Protection (OCHMO-TB-008 Rev A)
projectRefs: Link et al. 2018, Scientific Reports 8:120 (published BASS-II spread rates, Table S1)
Bhattacharjee et al. 2017, Fire Safety Journal (image-analysis error formula)
Giassi et al., NTRS 20160012298 (DSLR blue channel and CH* emission)
Google Gemini API (SI: drafts Ask answers; code checks every number)
Claude and Claude Code, Anthropic (SI: framing, much of the code)
Codex and ChatGPT, OpenAI (SI: code, demo video review)
Where the ISS at? API (live ISS position on /story)
JAXA FLARE experiment page (context only, no JAXA data used)
Ignos source code (MIT); libraries: numpy, scipy, rawpy, React, Vite, Plotly, three.js
